_meta.purpose: Curated neurological disease knowledge base seed for NEURO-MAS. Structured summaries only (no copied guideline text), per sources_and_licenses.txt.
_meta.review_status: PROTOTYPE - pending clinician verification before any clinical use
primary_sources: WHO ICD-10-CM (verified codes only; ICD-11 codes left pending explicit verification)
Orphanet/Orphadata (https://www.orpha.net) - orpha_code fields left PENDING where not individually verified against Orphadata to avoid fabricated identifiers

diseases.definition: A chronic neurological condition characterized by a predisposition to recurrent, unprovoked seizures caused by abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity in the brain.
diseases.age_of_onset: Bimodal: childhood and older adulthood, but can begin at any age
diseases.epidemiology: One of the most common serious neurological conditions worldwide; WHO estimates tens of millions of people are affected globally (exact prevalence varies by region and case definition - verify current WHO figure before citing precisely)
diseases.natural_history: Course is highly variable: some patients achieve seizure freedom with medication, others develop drug-resistant (intractable) epilepsy
diagnostic_methods: Clinical history and eyewitness seizure description
Basic metabolic/toxicology workup to exclude provoked causes
red_flags: Status epilepticus (seizure >5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery)
First seizure with focal neurological deficit
Seizure with fever and altered consciousness (possible CNS infection)
Post-traumatic seizure
diseases.emergency_criteria: Convulsive status epilepticus is a medical emergency requiring immediate care; NEURO-MAS treats this as an automatic Level 4 escalation trigger, never an autonomous treatment decision.
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - anti-seizure medication selection and dosing must follow current AAN/ILAE guidelines and clinician judgment; NEURO-MAS does not recommend specific drugs or doses
diseases.contraindications: Medication-specific; must be checked against current prescribing information and patient allergy/comorbidity profile by a clinician
diseases.prognosis: Variable; roughly two-thirds of patients achieve long-term seizure control with appropriate treatment
complications: SUDEP (sudden unexpected death in epilepsy) in a minority of cases

diseases.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, characterized clinically by bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity, along with a range of non-motor features.
genes: Most cases sporadic; GBA and LRRK2 variants are known genetic risk factors; SNCA, PRKN, PINK1 implicated in rarer familial forms
diseases.inheritance: Predominantly sporadic; a minority of cases show autosomal dominant or recessive inheritance patterns
diseases.age_of_onset: Typically after age 60, though early-onset forms exist
diseases.epidemiology: One of the most common neurodegenerative disorders after Alzheimer's disease; prevalence increases with age
diseases.natural_history: Slowly progressive over years to decades; motor fluctuations (ON/OFF phenomena) and dyskinesias often emerge after years of levodopa therapy
diagnostic_methods: Clinical diagnostic criteria (e.g., MDS clinical diagnostic criteria)
MRI to exclude other causes of parkinsonism
red_flags: Rapid progression / early falls (consider atypical parkinsonism)
Poor or absent levodopa response
Early autonomic failure or dementia
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - dopaminergic and adjunct therapy selection/dosing requires clinician management; NEURO-MAS surfaces adherence and symptom trend data only
diseases.contraindications: Medication-specific; check against current prescribing information
diseases.prognosis: Chronic and progressive; life expectancy close to general population with modern management, but functional decline occurs over time
complications: Dementia (in later stages for a subset of patients)

diseases.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative disease and the most common cause of dementia, characterized pathologically by amyloid-beta plaques and neurofibrillary tau tangles, and clinically by progressive decline in memory and other cognitive domains.
genes: APOE e4 allele is a major genetic risk factor for late-onset disease; APP, PSEN1, PSEN2 mutations cause rare early-onset familial Alzheimer's disease
diseases.inheritance: Late-onset: complex/multifactorial (APOE e4 risk allele); early-onset familial forms: autosomal dominant
diseases.age_of_onset: Typically after age 65 (late-onset); rare early-onset familial forms before age 65
diseases.epidemiology: The most common cause of dementia; prevalence rises sharply with age
diseases.natural_history: Gradual progression through stages often described as mild, moderate, and severe, with increasing loss of independence
diagnostic_methods: Clinical history from patient and informant
MRI to assess atrophy pattern and exclude other causes
CSF or PET biomarkers where available
Laboratory workup to exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline
red_flags: Rapidly progressive cognitive decline (days-weeks) - consider alternative diagnosis (e.g., encephalitis, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease)
New focal neurological deficits
Sudden behavioral change with acute confusion (possible delirium/infection)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - cholinesterase inhibitors, memantine, and disease-modifying antibody therapies require clinician evaluation and monitoring per current guidelines
diseases.prognosis: Progressive and currently not curable; disease-modifying and symptomatic treatments can slow or manage symptoms in some patients

diseases.definition: Acute focal neurological injury caused by interruption of blood supply to a region of the brain, most commonly due to thromboembolic occlusion of a cerebral artery.
symptoms: Sudden severe headache (more typical of hemorrhagic stroke)
diseases.age_of_onset: Risk increases with age; can occur at any age, especially with risk factors like atrial fibrillation, hypertension, or hypercoagulable states
diseases.epidemiology: A leading cause of long-term disability; ischemic strokes account for the majority of stroke cases
diseases.natural_history: Acute event followed by a recovery/rehabilitation phase of variable length; risk of recurrence persists and is modifiable through risk-factor control
diseases.orpha_code: N/A - common complex disease, not typically an Orphanet rare-disease entry
diagnostic_methods: Cardiac workup for embolic source (ECG, echocardiogram)
red_flags: FAST-positive presentation (Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services) - deterministic emergency trigger, not an AI judgment call
Sudden 'worst headache of life' (consider hemorrhage/SAH)
Fluctuating or worsening deficits
diseases.emergency_criteria: Any acute FAST-positive presentation is treated by NEURO-MAS as an automatic Level 4 escalation to emergency services; time-critical, never delayed for agent consensus.
monitoring: Blood pressure and risk-factor control adherence
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - acute reperfusion therapy (thrombolysis/thrombectomy) and secondary prevention are time-critical clinical decisions outside NEURO-MAS's scope; the system supports monitoring and recovery tracking only
diseases.monitoring_note: Recovery/rehabilitation monitoring is the appropriate NEURO-MAS use case, not acute triage
diseases.prognosis: Highly dependent on infarct size/location and time-to-treatment; ranges from full recovery to permanent disability

diseases.definition: Damage to peripheral nerves causing sensory, motor, and/or autonomic dysfunction, commonly distal and symmetric; diabetes mellitus is among the most common causes.
diseases.age_of_onset: Variable; diabetic neuropathy risk increases with diabetes duration and glycemic control
diseases.epidemiology: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is among the most common peripheral neuropathies worldwide, affecting a substantial proportion of long-standing diabetics
diseases.natural_history: Typically slowly progressive; course depends on underlying cause and its control (e.g., glycemic control in diabetes)
diseases.orpha_code: PENDING_VERIFICATION (varies by specific hereditary subtype, e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth)
diagnostic_methods: Skin biopsy for small-fiber neuropathy in select cases
red_flags: Rapidly ascending weakness (consider Guillain-Barre syndrome - emergency)
Asymmetric or rapidly progressive pattern (consider alternative diagnosis)
New autonomic symptoms (consider broader workup)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - pain management and disease-modifying treatment (e.g., glycemic control) require clinician oversight
diseases.prognosis: Variable; often manageable but not always reversible, especially with prolonged nerve damage

diseases.definition: An immune-mediated disease of the central nervous system involving inflammatory demyelination and neurodegeneration, with a clinical course that may be relapsing-remitting or progressive.
diseases.epidemiology: One of the most common causes of non-traumatic neurological disability in young adults; prevalence varies substantially by geography
diseases.natural_history: Relapsing-remitting course in most patients at onset; a proportion transition to secondary progressive disease over time
red_flags: Rapidly progressive brainstem/spinal cord symptoms
Signs suggestive of neuromyelitis optica (severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion)
monitoring: Disability scale trends (e.g., EDSS, tracked by clinician)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - disease-modifying therapy selection requires neurologist management
diseases.prognosis: Highly variable; many patients maintain good functional status for years with modern disease-modifying therapy
complications: Progressive disability in a subset of patients

diseases.definition: A progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting upper and lower motor neurons, leading to progressive muscle weakness, atrophy, and eventually respiratory failure.
symptoms: Respiratory muscle weakness in later stages
genes: C9orf72, SOD1, TARDBP, FUS implicated in familial ALS (~10% of cases); most cases sporadic
diseases.inheritance: Mostly sporadic; familial forms typically autosomal dominant
diseases.epidemiology: A rare but uniformly serious motor neuron disease
diseases.natural_history: Relentlessly progressive; median survival is commonly cited as roughly 2-5 years from symptom onset, though course varies considerably
diagnostic_methods: Clinical exam (upper + lower motor neuron signs)
red_flags: Rapid respiratory decline
Significant dysphagia with aspiration risk
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - disease-modifying and symptomatic therapy requires specialist multidisciplinary ALS clinic management
diseases.prognosis: Poor; disease is currently not curable, though multidisciplinary care and some therapies can extend survival/quality of life

diseases.definition: An autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the HTT gene, characterized by progressive motor (chorea), cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms.
diseases.natural_history: Progressive over 15-20 years typically, with motor, cognitive, and psychiatric decline
red_flags: Suicidality (psychiatric symptoms are common and serious)
Rapid functional decline
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - symptomatic treatment (e.g., for chorea, psychiatric symptoms) requires specialist management; genetic counseling implications require clinician/genetic counselor involvement
diseases.prognosis: Progressive and currently not curable; care is supportive and symptomatic

diseases.definition: An autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction, most commonly caused by antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, leading to fluctuating, fatigable muscle weakness.
symptoms: Fatigable limb weakness (worsens with activity, improves with rest)
diseases.epidemiology: An uncommon but well-characterized autoimmune neuromuscular disease
diseases.natural_history: Fluctuating course; can be well-controlled with treatment, but myasthenic crisis is a life-threatening complication
diagnostic_methods: CT chest to evaluate for thymoma
red_flags: Respiratory distress / myasthenic crisis - emergency
Rapidly worsening bulbar symptoms (aspiration risk)
diseases.emergency_criteria: Signs of respiratory compromise or myasthenic crisis are treated as an automatic Level 4 escalation, never resolved by agent consensus alone.
monitoring: Medication timing adherence (e.g., pyridostigmine dosing schedule, clinician-managed)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - immunosuppressive and symptomatic therapy requires specialist management
diseases.prognosis: Generally good with modern treatment; most patients achieve significant symptom control

diseases.definition: An acute, immune-mediated polyneuropathy, often post-infectious, causing rapidly progressive, typically ascending, weakness and areflexia.
symptoms: Respiratory muscle weakness in severe cases
diseases.age_of_onset: Can occur at any age; often preceded by a respiratory or gastrointestinal infection
diseases.epidemiology: A rare but medically significant acute neuropathy and a leading cause of acute flaccid paralysis worldwide
diseases.natural_history: Rapid progression over days to a few weeks, followed by a plateau and gradual recovery over months; a minority have residual deficits
red_flags: Rapidly ascending weakness
Respiratory muscle weakness / declining vital capacity
Autonomic instability (arrhythmia, blood pressure swings)
diseases.emergency_criteria: GBS with respiratory or autonomic compromise is a medical emergency; NEURO-MAS treats rapidly ascending weakness as an automatic Level 4 escalation trigger.
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - IVIG/plasma exchange decisions and respiratory monitoring require inpatient specialist care; NEURO-MAS is not appropriate for acute GBS triage, only recovery-phase monitoring
diseases.prognosis: Most patients recover substantially over weeks to months; a minority have long-term residual weakness

diseases.definition: A recurrent primary headache disorder characterized by moderate-to-severe, often unilateral, pulsating headache attacks, commonly accompanied by nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia, and sometimes preceded by a reversible aura.
symptoms: Sensory or speech aura in some patients
diseases.age_of_onset: Often begins in adolescence or early adulthood; more common in women after puberty
diseases.epidemiology: One of the most common primary headache disorders worldwide; affects a substantial proportion of adults, more common in women
diseases.natural_history: Episodic in most patients; a subset progress to chronic migraine (headache on 15 or more days per month)
diseases.orpha_code: N/A - common complex disease, not typically an Orphanet rare-disease entry
diagnostic_methods: Clinical history per ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria
Neurological exam to exclude secondary causes
Neuroimaging only if atypical features or red flags are present
differential_diagnoses: Secondary headache (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage, mass lesion)
Transient ischemic attack (when aura is present)
red_flags: Sudden 'thunderclap' headache (possible subarachnoid hemorrhage)
New headache after age 50
Headache with fever and neck stiffness (possible meningitis)
Focal neurological deficit atypical for the patient's usual aura
Headache with papilledema or that worsens with position change
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - acute and preventive medication selection must follow current AHS/AAN guidelines and clinician judgment; NEURO-MAS does not recommend specific drugs or doses
diseases.prognosis: Generally good with appropriate management; some patients experience long-term reduction in frequency, others develop chronic migraine

diseases.definition: An acute, typically unilateral, idiopathic peripheral facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) palsy causing sudden weakness or paralysis of the muscles of facial expression, often attributed to viral reactivation and nerve inflammation.
symptoms: Inability to fully close the eye on the affected side
Drooling or difficulty with facial movements
Altered taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue in some cases
Ear pain preceding onset in some cases
diseases.age_of_onset: Can occur at any age; peak incidence in adults 15-45
diseases.epidemiology: One of the most common causes of acute facial paralysis
diseases.natural_history: Typically peaks within 72 hours; most patients begin recovering within weeks, with a majority achieving substantial or full recovery over months
diseases.orpha_code: N/A - common condition, not typically an Orphanet rare-disease entry
diagnostic_methods: Clinical exam distinguishing peripheral (forehead involved) from central (forehead spared) facial weakness
Exclusion of other causes (stroke, Lyme disease, Ramsay Hunt syndrome, tumor)
MRI if presentation is atypical or there is no improvement
Electrophysiological testing in select prognostic cases
differential_diagnoses: Stroke (central facial weakness spares the forehead)
Guillain-Barre syndrome (Miller Fisher variant, if bilateral)
red_flags: Forehead sparing (suggests central/stroke cause, not Bell's palsy - urgent stroke workup)
Bilateral facial weakness (consider GBS or other systemic cause)
Vesicular rash in the ear canal (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
Gradual onset over weeks (consider tumor rather than Bell's palsy)
monitoring: Facial function grading trend (e.g., House-Brackmann, clinician-assessed)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - corticosteroid and antiviral therapy decisions require clinician evaluation, ideally within 72 hours of onset per current guidelines
diseases.prognosis: Favorable overall; most patients recover significant or full function, though a minority have residual weakness or synkinesis
complications: Exposure keratopathy / corneal damage from incomplete eye closure

diseases.definition: A transient episode of focal neurological dysfunction caused by brief interruption of blood flow to the brain, spinal cord, or retina, without evidence of acute infarction on imaging, with symptoms typically resolving within minutes to an hour.
symptoms: Symptoms fully resolve, typically within 1 hour
diseases.age_of_onset: Risk increases with age and shares risk factors with ischemic stroke (hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking)
diseases.epidemiology: A significant warning sign for stroke; a substantial proportion of TIA patients go on to have a stroke within days if untreated, making rapid evaluation critical
diseases.natural_history: Symptoms resolve completely by definition, but TIA carries a high short-term risk of subsequent stroke, especially in the first 48 hours
diseases.orpha_code: N/A - common complex disease, not typically an Orphanet rare-disease entry
diagnostic_methods: Urgent clinical evaluation (e.g., ABCD2-style risk stratification, clinician-applied)
CT/MRI brain to exclude infarction or hemorrhage
Cardiac workup for embolic source (ECG, echocardiogram, extended rhythm monitoring)
red_flags: Any FAST-positive presentation, even if resolved, requires urgent same-day evaluation
Crescendo TIAs (multiple episodes in short succession)
Known atrial fibrillation or high-grade carotid stenosis
diseases.emergency_criteria: NEURO-MAS treats any reported transient focal neurological deficit as an automatic Level 4 escalation to urgent medical evaluation, since TIA cannot be reliably distinguished from evolving stroke outside a clinical setting and short-term stroke risk after TIA is high.
monitoring: Risk-factor control adherence (blood pressure, glucose, anticoagulation if indicated)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - antiplatelet/anticoagulant therapy and urgent specialist referral decisions require clinician evaluation; NEURO-MAS does not triage acute TIA autonomously
diseases.prognosis: Variable; risk of subsequent stroke is highest in the days immediately following a TIA and is substantially reduced by prompt evaluation and risk-factor management

diseases.definition: A common progressive neurological disorder characterized primarily by bilateral action tremor of the hands and arms, often also affecting the head, voice, or other body regions, in the absence of other identifiable causes such as Parkinson's disease.
symptoms: Bilateral postural/kinetic hand tremor (worsens with action, improves at rest)
Tremor worsened by stress, caffeine, or fatigue
Improvement with small amounts of alcohol in many patients
genes: Familial clustering is common; specific causative genes are not consistently established, likely polygenic/heterogeneous
diseases.inheritance: Often familial with autosomal dominant-like clustering in some families, but genetics are complex and not fully characterized
diseases.age_of_onset: Bimodal: can begin in young adulthood or later life, with increasing prevalence with age
diseases.epidemiology: One of the most common movement disorders, considerably more common than Parkinson's disease
diseases.natural_history: Slowly progressive over years to decades; severity and functional impact vary widely
diagnostic_methods: Clinical history and examination (characteristic action tremor pattern)
Exclusion of Parkinson's disease and other causes (medication review, thyroid function)
DaTscan only if parkinsonism is suspected clinically
differential_diagnoses: Enhanced physiologic tremor (e.g., from medications, hyperthyroidism, caffeine)
red_flags: Rest tremor or asymmetric onset (consider Parkinson's disease)
Rapid progression or additional neurological signs (consider alternative diagnosis)
Tremor with gait/balance impairment out of proportion to typical essential tremor
monitoring: Impact on activities of daily living (writing, eating, drinking)
Alcohol use pattern (given symptomatic overlap with self-medication)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - beta-blocker, primidone, or other medication and procedural (e.g., focused ultrasound) decisions require clinician evaluation
diseases.prognosis: Generally not life-threatening; can progressively affect quality of life and functional independence in some patients
complications: Fall risk if head/gait involvement is present

diseases.definition: Inflammation of the meninges surrounding the brain and spinal cord, most commonly caused by bacterial or viral infection, ranging from a self-limited viral illness to a rapidly fatal bacterial emergency.
symptoms: Petechial or purpuric rash (suggestive of meningococcal disease)
diseases.age_of_onset: Can occur at any age; specific pathogens and risk profiles vary by age group (e.g., neonates, young adults in congregate settings, older adults)
diseases.epidemiology: Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency with significant mortality and morbidity if untreated; viral meningitis is more common and generally self-limited
diseases.natural_history: Bacterial meningitis progresses rapidly over hours and is life-threatening without prompt treatment; viral meningitis typically resolves over days to about two weeks
diseases.orpha_code: N/A - common infectious disease presentation, not an Orphanet rare-disease entry
diagnostic_methods: Lumbar puncture with CSF analysis (cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, PCR)
CT head prior to LP if signs of raised intracranial pressure or focal deficit
red_flags: Fever with neck stiffness and altered consciousness - medical emergency
Petechial/purpuric rash with fever (possible meningococcemia)
Rapidly decreasing level of consciousness
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (severe headache, vomiting, papilledema)
diseases.emergency_criteria: Suspected bacterial meningitis is a time-critical medical emergency; NEURO-MAS treats fever with neck stiffness and altered mental status as an automatic Level 4 escalation to emergency care, never delayed for agent consensus.
monitoring: Not appropriate for acute presentation - NEURO-MAS is not designed for acute meningitis triage
Post-recovery neurological/cognitive follow-up trend where relevant
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - suspected bacterial meningitis requires immediate empiric antibiotics and emergency care; this is outside NEURO-MAS's scope entirely and must never be delayed for AI-driven assessment
diseases.prognosis: Viral meningitis: generally good, full recovery typical. Bacterial meningitis: significant risk of mortality and long-term neurological sequelae even with treatment, dependent on how quickly treatment is started
complications: Death (particularly with bacterial meningitis if treatment is delayed)

diseases.definition: A chronic pain disorder affecting the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V), characterized by sudden, severe, brief episodes of electric shock-like facial pain, typically triggered by routine activities such as chewing, talking, or touching the face.
symptoms: Sudden severe electric shock-like facial pain
Pain confined to one or more trigeminal nerve branches, usually unilateral
Brief episodes lasting seconds to a couple of minutes
Pain triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, or wind on the face
diseases.age_of_onset: Most commonly begins after age 50, though it can occur earlier, especially in secondary cases (e.g., multiple sclerosis)
diseases.epidemiology: An uncommon but well-recognized cause of severe facial pain, more common in women and with increasing age
diseases.natural_history: Often relapsing-remitting, with episodes of frequent attacks separated by remission periods; can become more frequent or persistent over time in some patients
diagnostic_methods: Clinical history (characteristic trigger-evoked, brief, severe unilateral facial pain)
MRI brain to identify neurovascular compression or exclude secondary causes (e.g., multiple sclerosis, tumor)
Neurological exam, typically normal in classic/idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia
differential_diagnoses: Secondary trigeminal neuralgia (e.g., from multiple sclerosis or tumor)
red_flags: Sensory loss or numbness on exam (atypical for classic TN, suggests secondary cause)
Bilateral symptoms (consider multiple sclerosis or other secondary cause)
Onset in a young patient (consider MS workup)
Additional cranial nerve deficits
monitoring: Impact on eating/oral hygiene (trigger avoidance can affect nutrition and dental care)
diseases.treatment_status: GUIDELINE_REQUIRED - anticonvulsant medication (e.g., carbamazepine) and procedural/surgical options require clinician evaluation; NEURO-MAS does not recommend specific drugs or doses
diseases.prognosis: Variable; many patients achieve good pain control with medication, though some develop medication-resistant pain requiring procedural intervention
complications: Reduced oral intake/weight loss from trigger avoidance
